'''Millie Louise Bown Russell''' (October 29, 1926 – November 1, 2021) was an American health educator and college administrator based in Seattle. Much of her work as an administrator at the [[University of Washington]] involved expanding opportunities for minority students in the [[STEM pipeline]].

== Early life and education ==
Millie Bown was raised in the Seattle area, the daughter of Augustus Bown and Edith Ruth Cahill Bown. Her parents were politically active, and welcomed [[Paul Robeson]] and [[Marian Anderson]] as guests in their home.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2021-11-13 |title=Millie Russell, trailblazing Seattle medical educator and civil rights activist, dies at 95 |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/obituaries/dr-millie-russell-trailblazing-seattle-medical-educator-and-civil-rights-activist-dies-at-95/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |website=The Seattle Times |language=en-US}}</ref> One of her sisters was jazz pianist [[Patti Bown]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Dr. Millie L.B. Russell |url=https://bonneywatson.com/obituary/dr-millie-l-b-russell/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |website=Bonney Watson Funeral Home |language=en-US}}</ref>

Bown was an athletic young woman, and especially excelled at archery and dance in her teens.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1940-06-21 |title=Phyllis Wheatley |pages=2 |work=The Northwest Enterprise |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/117800398/phyllis-wheatley/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=1940-07-05 |title=Y.W.C.A. News |pages=2 |work=The Northwest Enterprise |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/117800629/ywca-news/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She earned a bachelor's degree in medical technology from [[Seattle University]] in 1948.<ref>Seattle University, ''[https://scholarworks.seattleu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1011&context=aegis The Aegis]'' (1948 yearbook): 31.</ref> She was the second Black student to enroll, after [[Sam Smith (American politician)|Sam Smith]], and the first to graduate.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=1933-1948: Depression, War and Peace |url=http://www.seattleu.edu/history/section4.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150302042042/http://www.seattleu.edu/history/section4.html |archive-date=2015-03-02 |access-date=2025-10-04 |website=Seattle University}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Srinivasan |first=Tanvi |date=February 10, 2023 |title=Notable Black Seattleites You Should Know About |url=https://www.seattlemet.com/news-and-city-life/influential-famous-notable-black-figures-seattle-history |access-date=2025-10-04 |website=Seattle Met |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1971 Russell earned a teaching certificate from the same school. She earned a master's degree in [[kinesiology]] in 1978 from the [[University of Washington]], and completed doctoral studies in education at the University of Washington when she was 62 years old, in 1988.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Remembering Dr. Millie Bown Russell |url=https://www.washington.edu/omad/2021/11/05/remembering-dr-millie-bown-russell/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |website=Office of Minority Affairs & Diversity |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-19 |title=In Memoriam: Millie Louise Bown Russell, 1926-2021 |url=https://www.jbhe.com/2021/11/in-memoriam-millie-louise-bown-russell-1926-2021/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |website=The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education}}</ref>

Bown became a member of [[Alpha Kappa Alpha]] in 1945.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1945-09-12 |title=Alpha Kappa Alpha Initiates Five |pages=1 |work=The Northwest Enterprise |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/117801063/alpha-kappa-alpha-initiates-five/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She represented the Seattle Youth Council of the [[NAACP]] at a national meeting in New Orleans in 1946.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1946-11-27 |title=Youth Council NAACP |pages=1 |work=The Northwest Enterprise |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/117800886/youth-council-naacp/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>  "Civil rights was important, and that was my volunteer work," she recalled later, "but I also liked health care and I liked making precise decisions about what is important for a person’s health care needs."<ref name=":2" />

== Career ==
Russell trained hematologists at the King County Central Blood Bank and the Puget Sound Regional Blood Center.<ref name=":1" /> Beginning in 1974, she worked at the University of Washington, as director of the pre-professional program for minority students interested in healthcare careers. She also taught biology courses and was assistant to the university's vice president in the Office of Minority Affairs. She founded the school's Early Scholars Outreach Program, and helped to develop the Ron McNair Seattle Science Center Camp-in event.<ref name=":1" />

Russell received the Charles E. Odegaard Award in 1981, for her work on behalf of minority students in [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]] fields. In 1989, she ran for a seat on the Seattle School Board.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1989-09-15 |title=Millie Russell campaign advertisement |pages=25 |work=Seattle Gay News |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/117802119/millie-russell-campaign-advertisement/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> "The factors for an effective school are well-known," she said in a newspaper interview that year. "We just have to be willing to design it. If we don't really invest in that, we're not really caring about America."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Halper |first=Leah |date=1989-06-24 |title=Busing is a Tool in Teaching of Diversity, Educator Says |pages=11 |work=The News Tribune |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/117802327/busing-is-a-tool-in-teaching-of/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> October 29, 2001, her 75th birthday, was declared Dr. Millie Russell Day by the Mayor of Seattle. She retired from the university in 2007.<ref name=":2" />

== Personal life and legacy ==
Millie Bown married Edward A. Russell Jr. in 1952. They had three children, Pat, Peter, and Paul.<ref name=":1" /> Her husband died in 2007, and Russell died in 2021, at the age of 95, in Seattle.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Millie Russell blazed a trail in medicine and became a mentor to many |url=https://magazine.washington.edu/feature/millie-russell-blazed-a-trail-in-medicine-and-became-a-mentor-to-many/ |access-date=2023-02-02 |website=UW Magazine — University of Washington Magazine}}</ref> The Dr. Millie Russell Endowed Scholarship aat the University of Washington is named in her honor, and it "benefits underrepresented, low-income, first-generation students interested in studying science".<ref name=":2" /> Her daughter Pat Russell is Executive Dean of the  Healthcare and Human Services division at Seattle Central College.
